analysis.one_liner: Penalizes wage theft, requires paystubs and timely final pay, and lets workers sue to recover stolen wages.
analysis.headline: The Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act was introduced in June 2026 with 26 Democratic cosponsors and has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill cracks down on wage theft — when employers don't pay workers for hours they worked. It would require employers to tell new hires their pay rate and job classification, issue itemized paystubs, and hand over final pay within 14 days of a job ending. It would double or triple the damages workers can win in court, ban employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims, extend the time workers have to sue from 2-3 years to 4-5 years, raise civil fines to as much as $250,000 per affected employee for repeat violators, and fund grants to community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are shorted on pay — particularly low-wage workers in industries like restaurants, retail, and construction, where the bill's own findings say nearly 20 percent of low-wage workers in the ten most populous states report being paid below minimum wage. Women, immigrants, and Black workers, who face minimum wage violations at higher rates, would also benefit from stronger recovery tools.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers who are shorted on pay

how_it_helps.text: Gives workers the right to the full pay rate in their contract, not just the federal minimum, and requires paystubs showing hours, rates, and deductions so violations can be spotted [S2].

Raises damages to twice unpaid wages plus interest, and triple wages for repeat offenders, and bans employers from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue in court as a condition of employment [S2].

Extends the window to sue from 2-3 years to 4-5 years and pauses the clock while the Labor Department investigates, lets workers get copies of their payroll records within 21 days, and makes falsifying wage records a crime subject to a mandatory Justice Department referral [S2].

Raises civil fines to up to $25,150 per employee per initial violation and $250,150 for repeat or willful violations, and funds grants to community organizations that help workers file claims and recover back pay [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who underpay workers — through back pay, doubled or tripled damages, higher fines, and possible criminal referral for falsified records. Law-abiding employers face new paperwork costs for disclosures and paystubs but gain a level playing field against cheaters.
analysis.who_pays_short: Noncompliant employers and their legal exposure

drawbacks.text: Small businesses face new administrative costs: written pay disclosures in the employee's language within 15 days of hire, updated disclosure when terms change, and detailed itemized paystubs for every pay period [S2].

Higher damages, a longer filing window, and a ban on arbitration make employer litigation exposure substantially larger, which supporters say is the deterrent and critics say raises business risk and costs that can be passed on [S2].
The grant program authorizes unlimited appropriations through fiscal year 2030, a new stream of federal spending for community organizations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance burden is real but modest relative to what the bill estimates is more than $50 billion a year taken from workers' paychecks. The strongest design feature is targeting the biggest enforcement gaps: weak damages, short deadlines, and arbitration agreements that let employers settle privately. The main cost — higher litigation and penalty exposure for employers — is largely the deterrent working as intended, though small businesses will feel the new paperwork rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote for the rest of the session so far.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 25, 2026, with 17 original cosponsors including the committee's ranking Democrat, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1][S4].
The bill gathered 26 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been taken on it since the referral [S3][S4].

The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to add pay disclosure, paystub, and final-pay requirements, raise damages and fines, ban mandatory arbitration of wage claims, extend the statute of limitations, and create a Labor Department grant program for community wage-theft enforcement [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who underpay workers, since the bill has not advanced and current penalties remain unchanged.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors

against.name: Tim Walberg
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican and has never reached the floor [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, staffing, agriculture, construction)
industries.note: These are the industries with the worst wage-and-hour compliance, and the bill triples damages, raises fines to $250,000 per employee for repeat offenders, and forces court access. Employers who underpay would pay more back wages and face more lawsuits.
The bill voids any agreement that makes workers give up their right to sue over wage claims, removing a tool that keeps wage disputes out of court.
The bill's own findings note that noncompliant competitors undercut honest employers on labor costs; higher penalties narrow that advantage.

industries.industry: Labor unions and nonprofit legal-aid and community organizations
industries.note: They are eligible for the new grant program to educate workers, help file claims, and assist enforcement, creating a funded role for them in wage enforcement.
New disclosure, paystub, and record-access requirements create demand for systems and services that help employers comply.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with no Republican support that has sat in committee since June typically dies there when the Congress ends in January 2027. Unless the committee schedules a hearing or markup in the remaining weeks, the bill will expire without a vote and would need to be reintroduced next Congress.
